tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, including possible mediators and connections to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to probe fundamental discrete symmetries through spin-dependent forces.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models of exotic boson-mediated spin-dependent interactions and surveys experimental techniques such as atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and precision spectroscopy.
result: Summarizes current constraints on coupling constants and mass ranges for various exotic bosons, and identifies promising future experimental directions.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a vibrant field with many open questions; further experimental and theoretical work is needed to discover or constrain new physics.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and soft matter systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, distinct from neighbor-based alignment.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental mechanism in active matter that can be harnessed for designing new materials and robotic systems.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, a soft matter physics study unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand memory effects in biopolymer networks far from equilibrium, which are relevant to biological tissues but not to the user's research interests.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory) is observed only in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics, but the work has no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental development of continuous thermochemical sources for AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors construct a compact AlF molecular beam oven using a thermochemical reaction between AlF3 and Al, and also demonstrate a dispenser source. They characterize brightness, rotational temperature, and velocity using spectroscopy and buffer gas cooling.
result: The oven achieves high brightness (10^11 molecules/sr/s) at 923 K, outperforming ablation-based sources for certain levels. Buffer gas cooling reduces rotational temperature to ~30 K and forward velocity to 200 m/s.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can provide high flux for laser cooling and trapping experiments, including potential direct loading of a magneto-optical trap.

title: Evolutionary Vaccination Dynamics Under Higher-order Reinforcement Pressure
authors: Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi And Yamir Moreno
abstract: Vaccination games in higher-order settings remain underexplored, despite their importance in shaping opinions and collective decisions. Here, we introduce a parsimonious behavioral-epidemiological model to evaluate how peer reinforcement influences vaccination uptake. The framework consists of a two-layer multiplex: an epidemic layer governed by the susceptible-infected-recovered process on a square lattice, and a behavioral layer represented by a hypergraph of triadic interactions. Individuals update their vaccination strategy via imitation, modulated by a reinforcement modulation parameter when local agreement with a like-minded peer is present. We find that higher-order structure alone induces clusters of vaccinated individuals that act as protective barriers. Small but nonzero values of ( ) maximize vaccination coverage and suppress outbreaks, while both the limiting case and larger values ( ) reduce uptake. This non-monotonic effect suggests that excessively strong local inhibition suppresses adaptability, whereas weaker inhibition facilitates the re-emergence of non-vaccinators. Our work bridges complex contagion theory with evolutionary game dynamics, offering insights into how contact structure and peer reinforcement jointly shape vaccination behavior.
tldr: This paper studies vaccination behavior on a multiplex network with higher-order interactions, using evolutionary game theory and epidemic modeling.
motivation: To understand how higher-order social reinforcement influences vaccination uptake and epidemic outcomes.
method: A two-layer multiplex model combining SIR epidemic dynamics on a square lattice with a hypergraph for triadic social interactions, where individuals update vaccination strategies via imitation with a reinforcement parameter.
result: Higher-order structure creates protective clusters; intermediate reinforcement maximizes vaccination coverage and suppresses outbreaks, while extreme values reduce uptake.
conclusion: Peer reinforcement in higher-order settings non-monotonically affects vaccination behavior, with implications for public health interventions.

motivation: Two-sample testing is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially for complex feature spaces where classical methods fail.

title: Omnidirectional Photonic Chiral Flatband In Nonlocal Membrane Metasurfaces
authors: Baohe Zhang, Jumin Qiu, Meng Qin, Haiyan Jiang, Shuyuan Xiao, Zhiwei Zheng, Leman Kuang, Hui Jing, Xinxing Zhou, Hongju Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Omnidirectional flat-band resonances, characterized by an enhanced photonic density of states and inherent angular robustness, are highly sought-after in integrated nanophotonic devices, particularly when integrated with chiral functionality. Here we realize such resonances in a nonlocal silicon membrane metasurface patterned with periodic square-lattice air-hole arrays. Increasing the lattice period not only compresses the Brillouin zone but, crucially, weakens the evanescent coupling between neighbouring Bloch modes associated with the same-order guided resonances. Driven by the tight-binding model in the limit of weak inter-unit-cell coupling, the pronounced band flattening of the degenerate guided resonance along both [MATH] and [MATH] yields, giving rise to an omnidirectional flat-band resonance. Remarkably, both numerical simulations and experiments reveal a universal route for endowing flat-band guided resonances with optical chirality through the deliberate breaking of the mirror symmetry of air holes. As a result, the omnidirectional chiral flat-band resonance emerges along both principal in-plane directions, with [MATH]-factors exceeding 10[MATH] and circular dichroism greater than 0.9 over a wide angular range of [MATH]. Nonlinear measurements further show that the resulting resonance not only drives highly efficient third-harmonic generation but also imparts a pronounced spin-selective character to the nonlinear process. Simultaneously, the highly efficient nonlinear process also enables chirality-controlled frequency-upconversion imaging. Our results establish a general paradigm for engineering omnidirectional chiral flat-band resonances in planar silicon platforms, opening new opportunities for nonlinear nanophotonics and chiral imaging.
tldr: This paper demonstrates omnidirectional chiral flat-band resonances in nonlocal silicon membrane metasurfaces for nonlinear nanophotonics and chiral imaging.
motivation: To achieve omnidirectional flat-band resonances with chiral functionality for integrated nanophotonic devices.
method: The authors use a nonlocal silicon membrane metasurface with periodic square-lattice air-hole arrays, breaking mirror symmetry to induce chirality, and employ tight-binding modeling and experiments.
result: They observe flat-band resonances with Q-factors >10^4 and circular dichroism >0.9 over a wide angular range, enabling efficient third-harmonic generation and chirality-controlled frequency-upconversion imaging.
conclusion: This work establishes a general paradigm for engineering omnidirectional chiral flat-band resonances in planar silicon platforms, opening opportunities for nonlinear nanophotonics and chiral imaging.

title: Design And Optimization Of An AZO-based Plasmonic Metasurface-driven Optical Solar Reflector For Thermal Management
authors: Lucas Viseur, Alexandre Mayer, Luc Henrard, Micha\"el Lobet
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plasmonic metasurface-driven Optical Solar Reflectors (m-OSRs) offer a promising route towards lightweight and high-performance thermal management. By exploiting subwavelength structuring and intrinsic material losses, such systems enable tailored absorptance spectrum across the solar and thermal infrared domains, respectively. Here, a plasmonic m-OSR composed of an aluminum back-reflector, a silicon dioxide dielectric spacer, and a nanostructured aluminum-doped zinc oxide (AZO) layer is investigated. The optical response of the structure is governed by the interplay between reflection, localized surface plasmon resonances and Fabry-Perot cavity effects, leading to efficient spectral selectivity. An optimization performed with a multi-objective genetic algorithm yields a low solar absorptance of alpha = 0.16 combined with a high thermal emissivity of epsilon = 0.83, providing an alpha/epsilon ratio of 0.19. These results highlight the potential of plasmonic meta-OSRs as ultrathin, high-performance solutions for thermal management and in particular for the next-generation advanced spacecraft.
tldr: This paper designs and optimizes an AZO-based plasmonic metasurface for thermal management in spacecraft, achieving low solar absorptance and high thermal emissivity.
motivation: Lightweight and efficient thermal management is critical for spacecraft, and traditional Optical Solar Reflectors (OSRs) are heavy. Plasmonic metasurfaces offer a promising alternative.
method: The authors simulate a multilayer structure (Al back-reflector, SiO2 spacer, nanostructured AZO) and use a multi-objective genetic algorithm to optimize the geometry for low solar absorptance and high thermal emissivity.
result: The optimized design achieves a solar absorptance of 0.16 and thermal emissivity of 0.83, yielding an alpha/epsilon ratio of 0.19.
conclusion: Plasmonic metasurface OSRs are ultrathin, high-performance solutions for spacecraft thermal management.

title: Exploring Fair Access To Quantum Computing
authors: Pieter Vermaas Benedict Lane
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This short article - commissioned as part of the Quantum Flagship project OpenSuperQPlus - introduces the topic of fair access to quantum computing time and argues for its relevance in current European technology policy debates. Choices about access we make today affect which applications of quantum computing are developed in the future, and by whom. Among the issues at stake are: Europe's technological autonomy and sovereignty; Europe's future economic competitiveness; knowledge security and the future of open science; and delivering upon the EU's founding values and aims. The results of a survey of OpenSuperQPlus researchers reveal prevalent contractualist and transactional framings of access to European quantum computing capacity among those developing the technology. The article concludes with a call to go beyond framing access to quantum computing as a zero-sum-game, and to explore the possibility of an access regime premised on openness and solidarity.
tldr: This paper discusses policy and ethical issues around fair access to quantum computing, not technical quantum research.
motivation: To argue for fair access to quantum computing resources in European policy debates.
method: Conceptual analysis and survey of researchers.
result: Identifies prevalent contractualist and transactional framings among researchers.
conclusion: Calls for an access regime based on openness and solidarity.

title: A Lattice-theoretic Framework For Hesitant Fuzzy Convexity Beyond Scalar Observables
authors: Carlos Salvatierra, Pedro Huidobro, Raquel Fernandez-Peralta
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In fuzzy-set theory, the notion of convexity has often been formulated through scalar reductions, typically via scores and aggregation functions. Although useful, such reductions may obscure relevant order-theoretic information in the codomain, especially in complex set-valued settings. This article develops a lattice-theoretic framework for convexity on lattice-valued mappings over point-convex segment-generated abstract convexity spaces. The framework separates the segment structure of the domain from the lattice structure of the codomain, distinguishing intrinsic convexity, defined through the lattice meet, from relational and observable convexities induced by preorders or scalar maps. The article characterizes when scalar observables preserve or reconstruct intrinsic convexity, and which codomain operators preserve it through their pointwise extensions. It then specializes the framework to hesitant fuzzy sets endowed with the symmetric lattice, recovering classical fuzzy and interval-valued convexities as natural restrictions. The structural result shows that the symmetric order cannot be represented by any finite family of scalar observables. This obstruction appears even on two-point typical hesitant fuzzy elements. Consequently, symmetric hesitant convexity cannot, in general, be reconstructed by any finite family of scalar observables. Moreover, every finite family of monotone scalar observables admits a three-point hesitant profile that is scalar-convex for all selected descriptions but not symmetrically convex.
tldr: This paper develops a lattice-theoretic framework for convexity in hesitant fuzzy sets, focusing on order-theoretic properties and the limitations of scalar observables.
motivation: Traditional scalar-based reductions of convexity in fuzzy set theory may lose order-theoretic information, especially in complex set-valued settings like hesitant fuzzy sets.
method: The authors separate the segment structure of the domain from the lattice structure of the codomain, defining intrinsic, relational, and observable convexities, and analyze when scalar observables preserve or reconstruct intrinsic convexity.
result: The symmetric order in hesitant fuzzy sets cannot be represented by any finite family of scalar observables, even on two-point elements, and there exist profiles that are scalar-convex but not symmetrically convex.
conclusion: The framework reveals fundamental limitations of scalar-based approaches to convexity in hesitant fuzzy sets, suggesting that richer lattice-theoretic methods are necessary.

title: The Dyadic Cauchy-Kernel Identity: Several Roads Back To Classical Objects
authors: Nicholas Castillo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This is an expository note. We take the dyadic Cauchy-kernel identity of Castillo-Costin-Costin, a global rational/factorial decomposition built on the polylogarithm, and follow it down several specializations. In each direction it returns to a classical landmark: the polylogarithm duplication formula and Hurwitz's Fourier-series formula; representations of the zeta function at the special argument pi and at rational arguments, in the neighborhood of Hurwitz's multiplication theorem; the Hasse-Sondow globally convergent series; and, through its discrete scale invariance, the extra zeros of the Dirichlet eta function together with the harmonic-sum asymptotics of Flajolet-Gourdon-Dumas, with Dirichlet L-values emerging as the amplitudes of a log-periodic oscillation. The aim is unification: to exhibit one compact identity as an organizing center from which these classical results may be read off. We claim no new theorems; where an identity may not previously have been displayed in exactly this form, we say so and explain why it is nonetheless a recombination of known ingredients.
tldr: An expository note showing how the dyadic Cauchy-kernel identity unifies several classical results in number theory and special functions.
motivation: To demonstrate that a single rational/factorial decomposition can serve as an organizing center for diverse classical identities.
method: The paper specializes the dyadic Cauchy-kernel identity to derive known formulas for polylogarithms, zeta functions, and Dirichlet L-values.
result: The identity reproduces the polylogarithm duplication formula, Hurwitz's Fourier-series formula, Hasse-Sondow series, and extra zeros of the Dirichlet eta function.
conclusion: The identity provides a unifying perspective but claims no new theorems; it is a recombination of known ingredients.

title: Structure-preserving Discretization And Fingering Dynamics Of A Cahn-Hilliard Model For Traction-driven Digit Morphogenesis
authors: Marvin Fritz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a Cahn-Hilliard equation with anisotropic traction flux arising as a reduced continuum model of mechanically biased cell interactions in digit-forming organoids. For a regularized problem with strictly positive bounded mobility, we introduce a mixed finite element discretization based on an implicit-explicit treatment of the chemical potential. We prove existence of discrete solutions, establish exact mass conservation and a discrete energy inequality, and show convergence of the fully discrete approximations to a weak solution of the regularized problem. Numerical experiments illustrate the resulting dynamics and show the transition from classical coarsening to traction-induced fingering and protrusive growth. The computational study is complemented by mass and energy diagnostics, an energy-balance residual, fingering-onset and protrusion-count diagnostics, and a manufactured-solution convergence study.
tldr: This paper presents a numerical analysis of a Cahn-Hilliard model for digit morphogenesis, focusing on structure-preserving discretization and fingering dynamics.
motivation: Understanding digit formation in organoids requires modeling cell interactions with mechanical bias, which this reduced continuum model aims to capture.
method: A mixed finite element discretization with implicit-explicit treatment of chemical potential is introduced, and convergence to weak solutions is proved.
result: Numerical experiments show transition from classical coarsening to traction-induced fingering and protrusive growth, with mass and energy diagnostics.
conclusion: The proposed discretization preserves mass and energy properties, and the model captures key morphogenetic dynamics.

title: On $m$-partial Isometries: Spectra, Weighted Shifts, And Similarity
authors: Mohamed Amine Aouichaoui, Micha{\l} Bucha{\l}a, Stephan Ramon Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The aim of this paper is to study [MATH]-partial isometries on Hilbert spaces, a natural extension of partial isometries and [MATH]-isometries. We establish structural and spectral results, characterize the [MATH]-partial isometric weighted shifts, and investigate similarity to [MATH]-isometries and [MATH]-partial isometries.
tldr: This paper studies m-partial isometries on Hilbert spaces, a purely mathematical topic with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To extend the theory of partial isometries and m-isometries to m-partial isometries, establishing structural and spectral results.
method: Functional analysis and operator theory techniques, including spectral analysis and characterization of weighted shifts.
result: Characterization of m-partial isometric weighted shifts and similarity conditions to m-isometries and m-partial isometries.
conclusion: The work contributes to operator theory but has no application to the user's research interests.

title: Characterizing Metric-space-valued Processes: Separating Classes And Weak Invariance Principles For Measure-theoretic Inference
authors: Anne van Delft
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article investigates stochastic processes taking values in metric spaces that lack a topological vector space structure, a regime characterized by intricate interplay between topological, geometric, and temporal dependence structures. It is formally established that spaces admitting an isometric Hilbertian embedding constitute a strict subclass within the much broader class of metric spaces possessing the ball property. While traditional kernel methods are susceptible to geometric distortion when the underlying space cannot be isometrically embedded into a Hilbert space, we bypass such limitations by exploiting a fundamental structural property inherent to this broader class; namely, that Borel probability measures are uniquely determined by their values on balls. These separating classes provide the foundation for the subsequently introduced measure-theoretic inference methodology. We derive uniform convergence of a family of time-dependent random measures, alongside weak invariance principles for the corresponding nonstationary random fields. This framework explicitly exposes how dependence and geometric complexity influence sample path regularity. Furthermore, because the rapid decay of small-ball probabilities can prohibit the existence of limiting distributions for supremum-based discrepancy measures, we develop [MATH]-based alternatives. By directly leveraging the introduced convergence results, this approach circumvents the need for higher-order [MATH]-process formulations. Finally, for spaces that do admit an isometric Hilbertian embedding, and where [MATH]-processes naturally arise, we establish limit theory for both degenerate and nondegenerate multi-parameter [MATH]-processes, and demonstrate that local discrepancy tests maintain asymptotic stability under dynamic parameter regimes.
tldr: This paper develops measure-theoretic inference for stochastic processes on metric spaces without vector space structure, focusing on separating classes and weak invariance principles.
motivation: Traditional kernel methods fail when the metric space cannot be isometrically embedded into a Hilbert space, motivating a new approach based on the ball property.
method: The authors exploit that Borel probability measures on such spaces are uniquely determined by their values on balls, and derive uniform convergence of time-dependent random measures and weak invariance principles.
result: They establish that spaces with isometric Hilbertian embedding are a strict subclass of those with the ball property, and develop U-process-based alternatives to supremum-based discrepancy measures.
conclusion: The framework provides a robust methodology for inference on metric-space-valued processes, with asymptotic stability under dynamic parameter regimes.

title: Twist Deformations For Hopf Coquasigroups
authors: Brais Ramos P\'erez Ram\'on Gonz\'alez Rodr\'iguez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop a general theory of twist deformations for Hopf coquasigroups in a symmetric monoidal category. To this end, we first introduce and study non-coassociative bimonoids endowed with left and right codivisions, and establish their connection with left and right Hopf coquasigroups. Next, motivated by the classical theory of Drinfeld twists for Hopf algebras, we define twists for non-coassociative bimonoids and prove that they induce deformations of Hopf coquasigroup structures through suitable modifications of the coproduct. In particular, we obtain explicit deformation procedures for right and left Hopf coquasigroups and analyze the corresponding antipodes. Finally, we apply the general theory to construct nontrivial examples arising from Hopf coquasigroups associated with the sphere [MATH], obtaining new examples of twisted Hopf coquasigroups that are neither commutative nor cocommutative.
tldr: Develops a theory of twist deformations for Hopf coquasigroups in symmetric monoidal categories, generalizing Drinfeld twists to non-coassociative settings.
motivation: To extend the classical theory of Drinfeld twists for Hopf algebras to Hopf coquasigroups, which are non-coassociative structures, and to construct new examples.
method: Introduces non-coassociative bimonoids with left and right codivisions, defines twists for them, and proves that twists induce deformations of Hopf coquasigroup structures via modified coproducts.
result: Obtains explicit deformation procedures for right and left Hopf coquasigroups and constructs nontrivial twisted examples from Hopf coquasigroups associated with the sphere.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for twist deformations in non-coassociative settings, yielding new non-commutative, non-cocommutative Hopf coquasigroups.

title: From Parameters To Feature Space: Task Arithmetic For Backdoor Mitigation In Model Merging
authors: Zhenqian Zhu, Yamin Hu, Yiya Diao, Weixiang Li, Haodong Li, Wenjian Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging (MM) has gained significant attention as a cost-effective approach to integrate multiple task-specific models into a unified model. However, recent work reveals that MM is highly susceptible to backdoor attacks. Existing defenses based on task arithmetic often fail to eliminate backdoors without substantially degrading clean-task performance, owing to their reliance on direct parameter-space editing. To address this gap, we propose Linear Feature Path Minimization (LFPM), a backdoor mitigation framework for model merging, which introduces an anti-backdoor task vector into the backdoored merged model. Unlike prior approaches, LFPM formulates the backdoor robustness of the merged model from a unified feature-space perspective under the Cross-Task Linearity (CTL) framework, which leverages the approximate linearity of features across tasks. This perspective guides the optimization of the anti-backdoor task to suppress backdoors while preserving clean-task performance. Furthermore, we introduce an effective optimization mechanism based on gradient accumulation and loss path-integral, ensuring robust backdoor suppression along the interpolation path. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFPM consistently exhibits strong robustness against backdoor attacks in both full fine-tuning and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) settings.
tldr: This paper proposes a backdoor mitigation framework for model merging in machine learning, using feature-space linearity to suppress backdoors while preserving clean-task performance.
motivation: Model merging is vulnerable to backdoor attacks, and existing parameter-space defenses degrade clean-task performance.
method: The authors introduce Linear Feature Path Minimization (LFPM), which optimizes an anti-backdoor task vector under the Cross-Task Linearity (CTL) framework using gradient accumulation and loss path-integral.
result: LFPM consistently shows strong robustness against backdoor attacks in both full fine-tuning and PEFT settings.
conclusion: Feature-space approaches can effectively mitigate backdoors in model merging without sacrificing clean-task accuracy.

title: The Switching Lemma Shows What The Switching Lemma Cannot Prove: An Unconditional Natural-proofs Barrier
authors: Bruno Loff, Suhail Sherif, Navid Talebanfard, Francesca Ugazio
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Razborov and Rudich (JCSS'97) observed that all known lower-bound proofs follow a certain pattern: when showing that a function [MATH] is hard, along the way the proof provides us with a distinguisher, namely, an efficient algorithm which can distinguish easy functions from random functions. They called such lower-bound proofs natural proofs. They then showed a natural-proofs barrier: under standard cryptographic assumptions, natural proofs cannot show superpolynomial lower-bounds against Boolean circuits. Along similar lines it can be shown that under a suitable cryptographic assumption, natural proofs cannot significantly improve the current state-of-the-art lower bound against constant depth circuits (AC0). The state of the art, using Hstad's Switching Lemma (SL), is [MATH] for depth-[MATH] circuits, and (conditionally) no natural proof can prove lower bounds of [MATH] for some large constant [MATH]. In this paper we revisit the natural-proofs barrier from an [MATH] perspective. We focus on AC0-natural proofs, i.e. proofs whose distinguishers are computable by AC0 circuits. Razborov and Rudich observed that lower bounds based on SL are AC0-natural. We show that this is true for most known lower-bound techniques against constant-depth circuits. We then establish an unconditional barrier for such proofs. By localizing the Trevisan--Xue pseudorandom generator, we are able to show that no AC0-natural proof can prove a lower bound greater than [MATH] against depth-[MATH] circuits. This is in the same quantitative regime as the SL frontier which instead has [MATH] in the power of [MATH]. The proof has a striking self-referential aspect: the proof of security of the Trevisan--Xue generator crucially relies on SL, and so SL has been used to show that AC0-natural proofs, such as SL itself, cannot prove AC0 lower bounds better than that of SL.
tldr: This paper proves an unconditional barrier for AC0-natural proofs, showing that such proofs cannot improve AC0 lower bounds beyond a certain threshold, using a self-referential argument that relies on the Switching Lemma itself.
motivation: To understand the limitations of natural proofs in complexity theory, specifically for constant-depth circuits, and to establish an unconditional barrier that does not rely on cryptographic assumptions.
method: The authors localize the Trevisan–Xue pseudorandom generator and use the Switching Lemma to prove that no AC0-natural proof can prove a lower bound greater than n^{log^{O(1)} n} against depth-d circuits.
result: They show that AC0-natural proofs cannot prove lower bounds beyond n^{log^{O(1)} n}, which is in the same regime as the current state-of-the-art from the Switching Lemma.
conclusion: The Switching Lemma itself cannot be used to prove significantly better AC0 lower bounds via natural proofs, establishing an unconditional barrier for such proof techniques.

title: An Assessment Framework For Application-Level Cryptographic Agility
authors: Gregoire Messmer Navaneeth Rameshan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The impending post-quantum transition to new cryptography will require complete replacement of algorithms within all software. The cryptographic APIs used today make this transition challenging because they were not designed with agility as a concern. There is no method for systematically assessing cryptographic agility as an overall ability. In addition to this, the term itself refers to multiple independent capabilities. Specifically, it includes replacing algorithms, selecting by policy, and substituting implementations. This lack of structured decomposition limits both the evaluation of systems and the development of cryptographically agile APIs. We introduce a component-based assessment framework that characterizes application-level cryptographic agility along seven orthogonal dimensions: three coupling dimensions that measure what the application code knows about algorithms and providers, a cross-cutting decoupling mechanism, a governance authority dimension, and two agility enablers that measure actual migration capability. The framework is non-linear and captures non-hierarchical profiles: a system may achieve high operation decoupling yet low creation decoupling, or strong versioning without externalized configuration. We evaluate six representative APIs (PKCS#11, OpenSSL~3.0, JCA, Google Tink, AWS KMS, and HashiCorp Vault Transit) against the framework, revealing three pervasive and independent gaps: no system supports intent-based key creation, none provides policy-driven algorithm selection (as distinct from access control), and none offers dedicated/first-class operations for algorithm transformation of existing keys. These gaps are individually sufficient to prevent agile migration, explaining why the post-quantum transition remains a software engineering problem despite decades of API progress.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for assessing cryptographic agility in software APIs, focusing on the post-quantum transition.
motivation: Current cryptographic APIs lack systematic support for algorithm replacement, policy selection, and implementation substitution, hindering the post-quantum transition.
method: The authors define seven orthogonal dimensions for agility assessment and evaluate six representative APIs against this framework.
result: Three pervasive gaps are identified: no intent-based key creation, no policy-driven algorithm selection, and no dedicated operations for key transformation.
conclusion: The framework reveals that these gaps individually prevent agile migration, explaining why the post-quantum transition remains a software engineering challenge.

title: A Near-quadratic Lower Bound On The Border Determinantal Complexity Of $\sum_i X_i^n$ Via Conormal Specialization
authors: Karthik Sheshadri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The border determinantal complexity [MATH] of a polynomial [MATH] is the least [MATH] such that [MATH] is a limit of determinants of [MATH] matrices of affine-linear forms. We prove that for every [MATH], over [MATH], \[ \dcb\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^n\Big)\ \ge\ {4e}, \qquad \sdcb\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^n\Big)\ \ge\ {2e} \] in the ordinary and symmetric models respectively; both match the known [MATH] upper bounds up to the constant. To our knowledge these are the first border determinantal lower bounds for an explicit family that are superlinear in the number of variables: the known quadratic border bound for the permanent reads the of the dual variety and is linear in its number of variables, whereas we transfer the dual . The proof has two ingredients. The first is an unconditional bound on the slot-[MATH] conormal multidegree of the multiplicity-one Gauss-graph cycle of an arbitrary affine-linear determinant -- singular, reducible, and non-reduced fibers allowed -- by a multihomogeneous B\'ezout count of a lifted kernel incidence. The second is a specialization argument: along any degeneration [MATH], the flat limit of these Gauss-graph cycles contains the conormal variety of the Fermat cone with positive coefficient. A cone-shift identity converts that conormal multidegree into the classical dual degree [MATH] of the smooth Fermat hypersurface, and an [MATH]-st root yields the quadratic bound. The exact lower bounds of the author's companion manuscripts follow as corollaries.
tldr: This paper proves near-quadratic lower bounds on the border determinantal complexity of the polynomial sum of n-th powers, using conormal specialization and dual variety techniques.
motivation: Understanding the computational complexity of polynomials is a central problem in algebraic complexity theory; border determinantal complexity measures the size of a determinantal representation needed to approximate a polynomial.
method: The proof combines an unconditional bound on the conormal multidegree of Gauss-graph cycles of affine-linear determinants with a specialization argument that relates the flat limit to the conormal variety of the Fermat cone, then uses a cone-shift identity to connect to the dual degree of the Fermat hypersurface.
result: Lower bounds of Ω(n^2) for ordinary border determinantal complexity and Ω(n^2) for symmetric border determinantal complexity are obtained, matching known upper bounds up to constants.
conclusion: These are the first superlinear border determinantal lower bounds for an explicit family, demonstrating the power of geometric methods in algebraic complexity.

title: Identifiability Without Gaussianity: Symbolic World Models And Near-Infinite Temporal Consistency
authors: {\l}ukasz Chmiel Seth Dobrin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12471v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Klindt, LeCun, and Balestriero (arXiv:2605.26379) proved that Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) achieve linear identifiability, the linear recovery of the world's true latent variables, if and only if the world's latent dynamics follow a Gaussian, stationary process. This Gaussian boundary implies a fundamental limit on temporal consistency: for any non-Gaussian physical system, the representation error of a statistical World Model grows monotonically with time. We prove that this limit is an artifact of the statistical alignment mechanism, not a property of World Models in general. We introduce the Physics-Grounded Symbolic Architecture (PGSA) and prove three results: (1) a PGSA achieves exact linear identifiability for all physical regimes, regardless of the latent distribution; (2) the per-step error of a PGSA is bounded by numerical precision alone; and (3) as a direct consequence, a PGSA maintains temporal consistency for an unbounded number of transitions, a property we term near-infinite temporal consistency. We further prove that statistical World Models cannot achieve this property for any non-Gaussian system, regardless of model capacity or the volume of training data. The algebraic cores of four of the theorems are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib4 v4.31.0 (zero sorry placeholders); the Klindt et al. converse is taken as an external premise. The contrast establishes that symbolic grounding in the causal generator of the world's dynamics is the sufficient condition and, in non-Gaussian regimes, the only condition for near-infinite temporal consistency.
tldr: The paper proves that symbolic world models achieve near-infinite temporal consistency for non-Gaussian systems, overcoming a fundamental limit of statistical world models.
motivation: Statistical world models fail for non-Gaussian dynamics, leading to growing representation error over time. The authors aim to show this limit is not fundamental and can be overcome by symbolic grounding.
method: The authors introduce the Physics-Grounded Symbolic Architecture (PGSA) and prove three theorems about identifiability, per-step error bounded by numerical precision, and near-infinite temporal consistency. Four theorems are formalized in Lean 4.
result: PGSA achieves exact linear identifiability for all physical regimes, per-step error bounded by numerical precision, and maintains temporal consistency for an unbounded number of transitions. Statistical world models cannot achieve this for non-Gaussian systems.
conclusion: Symbolic grounding in the causal generator of the world's dynamics is sufficient and, for non-Gaussian regimes, necessary for near-infinite temporal consistency.

title: Metasurfaces Bridge The Terahertz Gap
authors: Sarah Elghazoly
Euclides Almeida
abstract: Nature Photonics, Published online: 05 June 2026;
tldr: A nonlinear metasurface enables tunable continuous-wave terahertz emission at room temperature, bridging the terahertz gap.
motivation: The terahertz spectral region is difficult to access with compact, room-temperature sources; a practical solution is needed for applications in imaging, spectroscopy, and communications.
method: The authors design and fabricate a carefully engineered nonlinear metasurface that generates continuous-wave terahertz radiation via optical rectification or difference-frequency generation.
result: The metasurface achieves widely tunable, continuous-wave terahertz emission at room temperature, demonstrating a compact and efficient source.

title: Time-varying Photonics Enables Polarization Control
authors: Sangwan Sim
abstract: Nature Photonics, Published online: 05 June 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates dynamic polarization control using time-varying photonics in an epsilon-near-zero material.

title: The Costs And Benefits Of Physics Research
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 09 June 2026;
tldr: This paper discusses the environmental impacts and cost-benefit analysis of physics research in general, with no specific technical content.

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065403] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how charged semiflexible nanofibers affect water self-diffusion using NMR and simulations.
motivation: Understanding the nanoscale dynamics of water in dispersions of charged nanofibers is important for applications in materials science and rheology.
method: The authors use pulsed-field-gradient NMR to measure water self-diffusion coefficients and molecular dynamics simulations to interpret the results.
result: They find that the presence of charged nanofibers reduces water self-diffusion, with the effect depending on fiber concentration and charge density.
conclusion: The reduction in water mobility is attributed to electrostatic interactions and confinement effects, providing insights into the rheological behavior of such dispersions.

title: Vanishing Dynamic Strength Measured In A Transient High-pressure Phase Of Tin

This work reports two independent experimental estimations of the dynamic strength of the body-centered tetragonal (bct) [MATH] phase of tin, which occurs at pressures above about 9 GPa and transforms promptly back to the ambient [MATH] phase upon pressure release. Measuring strength in such a transient h…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065502] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper measures the dynamic strength of a transient high-pressure phase of tin, which is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Understanding the mechanical properties of materials under high pressure is important for applications like shock physics, but does not connect to the user's research interests.
method: Two independent experimental techniques were used to estimate the dynamic strength of the body-centered tetragonal phase of tin at pressures above 9 GPa.
result: The dynamic strength of the transient bct phase was measured and found to be vanishingly small.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into the mechanical behavior of tin under high pressure, but have no relevance to quantum information science or thermodynamics.

abstract:

Using a linear hydrodynamic model, we theoretically investigate the interaction between penetrating electron beams and sub-5-nm metallic spherical nanoparticles. We derive an analytical expression of the electron energy loss probability that includes nonlocal effects in the response of the confined …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023279] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron energy loss in metallic nanoparticles using a nonlocal hydrodynamic model, focusing on plasmon excitation.
motivation: To understand nonlocal effects in the optical response of sub-5-nm metallic nanoparticles when probed by penetrating electron beams.
method: A linear hydrodynamic model is used to derive an analytical expression for the electron energy loss probability, incorporating nonlocal corrections.
result: Analytical expressions for energy loss probability are obtained, showing how nonlocal effects modify the plasmonic response.
conclusion: Nonlocal effects are significant in small nanoparticles and must be accounted for in electron energy loss spectroscopy.

tldr: This paper studies membrane-associated self-assembly for cellular decision-making, a topic in biophysics and cellular signaling.

method: The authors use theoretical modeling and simulations to study self-assembly of membrane-associated proteins.
result: They show that self-assembly can act as a switch for cellular decision-making.

title: Visualizing Bulk Band Structure In ${\mathrm{Fe}}_{4}\mathrm{N}$ Thin Films By Spin- And Angle-resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy
authors: Karen Nakanishi, Masaaki Kakoki, Kiyotaka Ohwada, Kenta Kuroda, Kazuki Sumida, Hitoshi Sato, Koji Miyamoto, Taichi Okuda, Shinji Isogami, Keisuke Masuda, Yuya Sakuraba, And Akio Kimura

[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023257] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy to visualize the bulk band structure of ferromagnetic Fe4N thin films.
motivation: To understand the electronic structure of Fe4N, a promising spintronic material, by experimentally determining its bulk band structure and spin polarization.
method: Spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy with synchrotron radiation was performed on in situ prepared Fe4N thin films.
result: Most bands near the Fermi level are of minority spin, and the experimental band structure agrees well with first-principles calculations.
conclusion: The study provides a detailed experimental mapping of the spin-resolved band structure of Fe4N, confirming theoretical predictions and aiding spintronic applications.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
abstract:
Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding and mitigating anisotropy in silica films could improve detector performance.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to detect anisotropy and its response to heat treatment.
result: They find that silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, which has implications for coating design and postprocessing.
conclusion: The discovery informs strategies for coating deposition and postprocessing to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Stretching Theory Of Hookean Metashells
authors: Luca Giomi
abstract:

A continuum theory that describes how mechanical metamaterials deform on surfaces takes the form of the Schrödinger equation and provides a different path for materials design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021035] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: A continuum theory for mechanical metamaterials on surfaces is derived, taking the form of the Schrödinger equation.
motivation: To understand how mechanical metamaterials deform on curved surfaces and to provide a new design principle.
method: Develops a continuum theory that maps the deformation of Hookean metashells to a Schrödinger-like equation.
result: The theory yields a mathematical analogy between mechanical deformation and quantum mechanics.
conclusion: This approach offers a different path for designing mechanical metamaterials.

authors: I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, And G. Baldi

title: Seeing New Depths: Three-Dimensional Flow Of A Free-Swimming Alga
authors: Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, And Xiang Cheng

Experimental three-dimensional measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga reveal that microscopic organisms generate unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena, expanding our understanding of microhydrodynamics with profound biological implications for microbial motility and physiology.

method: Experimental three-dimensional flow measurements around a free-swimming alga using advanced imaging techniques.
result: Discovery of unexpected three-dimensional flow structures at low Reynolds numbers.
conclusion: The findings expand understanding of microhydrodynamics and have implications for microbial motility and physiology.

title: Subsurface Driven Size-Dependent Elasticity In Nanodiamond
authors: Jiaqi Zhang, Chunmeng Liu, Xing Li, Dongyang Wang, Keke Zhao, Houlin Ji, Yoshifumi Oshima, Shaobo Cheng, And Chongxin Shan
abstract:
Author(s): Jiaqi Zhang, Chunmeng Liu, Xing Li, Dongyang Wang, Keke Zhao, Houlin Ji, Yoshifumi Oshima, Shaobo Cheng, and Chongxin Shan

Subsurface compliant regions in nanodiamond allow for an elastic response to strain, providing a method for engineering the mechanical properties of brittle materials like diamond.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021010] Published Fri Apr 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies size-dependent elasticity in nanodiamond driven by subsurface compliant regions, focusing on mechanical properties of brittle materials.
motivation: Understanding and engineering the mechanical properties of diamond at the nanoscale is important for applications in nanomechanics and materials science.
method: The authors use experimental characterization and theoretical modeling to investigate how subsurface structures affect the elastic response of nanodiamond particles of varying sizes.
result: They find that subsurface compliant regions enable an elastic response to strain, leading to size-dependent elasticity that can be tuned.
conclusion: The work provides a method for engineering the mechanical properties of diamond, potentially expanding its use in nanoscale devices.

title: Active Hydrodynamic Theory Of Euchromatin And Heterochromatin
authors: S. Alex Rautu, Alexandra Zidovska, David Saintillan, And Michael J. Shelley
abstract:
Author(s): S. Alex Rautu, Alexandra Zidovska, David Saintillan, and Michael J. Shelley

Researchers develop a theoretical framework that shows how mechanical forces and flows drive the spatial segregation and nucleus-wide patterning of chromatin in cells.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021009] Published Thu Apr 09, 2026.
tldr: Develops an active hydrodynamic theory to explain the spatial segregation of euchromatin and heterochromatin in cell nuclei.
motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces and flows drive chromatin organization is crucial for cell biology, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors formulate a theoretical framework based on active hydrodynamics, modeling chromatin as an active fluid with differential activity and mechanical properties.
result: The model predicts that active stresses and flows lead to spontaneous segregation of euchromatin and heterochromatin, reproducing nuclear-scale patterns.
conclusion: Mechanical forces alone can drive chromatin compartmentalization, offering a physical mechanism for nuclear organization.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electric fields, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: A multi-step model involving surface defects, electrical stress, heating, and particle emission explains the onset of vacuum arcs.
conclusion: Improved understanding can lead to better design of accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and behavior.
motivation: Transplutonium elements are important for nuclear applications and exhibit unique electronic behavior due to 5f electrons at the boundary of localization and itinerancy.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical studies of metals, alloys, compounds, and coordination complexes under high pressure.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of how pressure affects the electronic structure, bonding, and phase transitions in these materials.
conclusion: High-pressure studies reveal complex behavior in transplutonium materials, advancing knowledge of heavy-element physics and chemistry.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and their multimessenger implications.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to nuclear astrophysics and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper surveys detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and discusses simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It highlights the potential for multimessenger observations to improve understanding of dense matter environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger astronomy with continuous gravitational waves will be a rich field for future detectors.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties provide crucial tests of nuclear physics under extreme conditions.
method: The paper reviews recent gravitational-wave detections from binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to theoretical predictions of the nuclear equation of state.
result: Observations constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, which are compared to extrapolations of nuclear equation of state models.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of dense matter, but the paper does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by John Hopfield reflecting on his career and the nature of physics as a point of view.
motivation: To share personal insights and perspectives on physics research, particularly in neural networks and associative memory.
method: Narrative and reflective lecture, not a technical research paper.
result: No new scientific results; the lecture discusses the evolution of ideas and the interdisciplinary nature of physics.
conclusion: Physics is a way of thinking that can inspire breakthroughs across disciplines, as exemplified by Hopfield's own work.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, a foundational concept in machine learning.
motivation: To present the historical development and significance of Boltzmann machines in the context of neural networks and artificial intelligence.
method: Lecture format, describing the conceptual framework and training algorithms for Boltzmann machines.
result: Boltzmann machines are stochastic neural networks capable of learning complex probability distributions, influencing deep learning.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, highlighting cases where techniques are combined.
result: The review demonstrates that these techniques can directly access atomic-scale disorder information, especially when used in combination.
conclusion: Combined real-space microscopy methods provide a more complete picture of defects in semiconductors, aiding materials science.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonances.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions in stars is crucial for stellar burning and element formation, but many reactions are difficult to measure directly.
method: Summarizes theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques.
result: Provides a comprehensive overview of the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory.
conclusion: The review highlights the importance of quantum phenomena in stellar nucleosynthesis and suggests new experimental approaches.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants.
motivation: Accurate and consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology.
method: A least-squares adjustment of all available experimental and theoretical data up to the end of 2022.
result: A self-consistent set of values and conversion factors for physics and chemistry.
conclusion: The CODATA 2022 values provide the most accurate and reliable constants for use in research and applications.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser-induced ultrasound to image deep tissues with optical contrast.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed to provide biological and clinical insight into cells and tissues, particularly for deep-tissue imaging with high resolution.
method: The paper reviews the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, where short laser pulses are absorbed by tissue, causing a temperature rise that generates ultrasound waves detected by external transducers.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables noninvasive imaging of optical contrast at depths of millimeters to centimeters with high resolution, and has been combined with optical techniques for multimodal imaging.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical research, offering deep-tissue imaging capabilities that complement traditional optical microscopy.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys various software packages and their interoperability, focusing on the generation and use of maximally localized Wannier functions.
result: It describes the ecosystem's capabilities for computing band structures, topological invariants, and other material properties.
conclusion: The Wannier-function approach is a powerful and widely used tool in condensed-matter physics, with a mature software ecosystem.

title: Kinetic Solitary Electrostatic Structures In Collisionless Plasma: Phase-space Holes
authors: I. H. Hutchinson
abstract:
Author(s): I. H. Hutchinson

Plasma is usually taught to be a quasineutral gas of charged and neutral particles that exhibits collective behavior. However, satellites regularly observe solitary potential structures in space plasmas that are isolated positive or negative potential humps, called electron or ion holes. In the 1970s, laboratory observations were made of electron holes. This review presents an overview of the observation of these electrostatic structures and presents their origin and their stability, using analytic theory and simulations. The role of kinetically unstable velocity distributions is identified as a key driver.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045007] Published Tue Dec 10, 2024.
tldr: A review of solitary electrostatic structures (phase-space holes) in collisionless plasma, covering observations, theory, and simulations.
motivation: To understand the origin and stability of isolated potential humps observed in space plasmas, which are not explained by standard quasineutral plasma theory.
method: Review of satellite observations, laboratory experiments, analytic theory, and particle-in-cell simulations of electron and ion holes.
result: Phase-space holes arise from kinetic instabilities in velocity distributions and can be stable over long times, explaining many space plasma observations.
conclusion: Kinetic solitary structures are a fundamental nonlinear phenomenon in collisionless plasmas, with implications for space weather and plasma diagnostics.

title: Atomic-scale 3d Insights Into Heteroepitaxial Mechanisms In Hcp/fcc, Bcc/fcc, And Fcc/fcc Core–shell Nanoparticles
authors: Xilong Mu, Yao Zhang, Kang’an Wang, Haoyi Tang, Zhiheng Xie, Zezhou Li, Xuemin Cao, Peng He And Jihan Zhou
abstract: Heteroepitaxy on nanocrystals of diverse crystal structures—hexagonal close-packed (hcp), body-centered cubic (bcc), and face-centered cubic (fcc)—is a powerful approach for engineering atomic arrangements. However, the mechanisms by which interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch remain poorly understood at the three-dimensional (3D) atomic scale. Here, we use atomic-resolution electron tomography to determine the 3D atomic structures and reveal heteroepitaxial mechanisms in Pt-based core–shell nanoparticles with diverse crystal structures including hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. We have identified distinct heteroepitaxial modes in these model systems, each mitigating the structural mismatch within a single particle: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, coherent growth with strain sharing between core and shell in bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and oriented growth combined with twin proliferation in decahedral fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. The various semi-coherent growth modes in the hcp/fcc nanoparticle yield a 3D dislocation network at a scale below 10 nm, interconnected by Lomer–Cottrell, Hirth, and Shockley dislocations. The key heteroepitaxial mechanisms in these examined systems are quantitatively validated by interfacial energies derived from molecular statics simulations. We anticipate these insights will inform the targeted design of interfacial structures and enable precise strain engineering in core–shell nanomaterials.
tldr: This paper uses atomic-resolution electron tomography to study heteroepitaxial mechanisms in core-shell nanoparticles with different crystal structures.
motivation: Understanding how interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch in heteroepitaxial nanoparticles is crucial for engineering atomic arrangements.
method: Atomic-resolution electron tomography was used to determine 3D atomic structures of Pt-based core-shell nanoparticles (hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, fcc/fcc Ru@Pt), combined with molecular statics simulations.
result: Distinct heteroepitaxial modes were identified: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc, coherent growth with strain sharing in bcc/fcc, and oriented growth with twin proliferation in fcc/fcc. A 3D dislocation network below 10 nm was observed.
conclusion: The findings provide insights for targeted design of interfacial structures and strain engineering in core-shell nanomaterials.

title: Mean Field Game Model Of The Impact Of Reductions In Support On Faculty Research Activity
authors: Robert A. Brownahttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing & Data Sciences, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceThe vibrancy of United States university science and engineering research depends on the competitive interactions of research faculty who win federal grants for support. Mean field game theory gives a framework for understanding the impact of ...
tldr: This paper uses mean field game theory to model the impact of reduced federal support on faculty research activity in US universities.
motivation: To understand how competitive interactions among research faculty affect the vibrancy of university science and engineering research under funding constraints.
method: Applies mean field game theory to model the strategic behavior of faculty competing for federal grants.
result: The model predicts changes in research activity levels and distribution in response to reductions in support.
conclusion: Mean field game theory provides a framework for analyzing policy impacts on research ecosystems.

title: Network-Based Multi-Layer Model Using Machine Learning For Optimal Vaccine Prioritization In Heterogeneous Populations
authors: Bernard Asamoah Afful Mordecai Opoku Ohemeng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work advances epidemic control beyond traditional mass vaccination models by integrating population heterogeneity, network structure, and machine-learning-based decision policies. Using the Email-Eu-core contact network, we compare classical centrality-driven vaccination strategies with graph neural network (GNN) and reinforcement learning (RL) approaches. Across 30 stochastic simulations, classical heuristics, including degree, betweenness, and layer-based vaccination, exhibit similar performance, reflecting the network's dense connectivity and modest community structure. In contrast, the GNN-based strategy substantially reduces peak infection, final epidemic size, and time to peak, demonstrating its ability to identify structurally critical nodes that classical metrics overlook.
